memories.memory_text: I held the elevator for a girl who looked about as sick as I felt, but she passed—then walked right into me. For a second, the world just stopped. I couldn’t look away.
I stood next to her after group and just said it—'What's your name?'—then told her she was beautiful, because she was, and I wasn't going to pretend I didn't see it.
I remember holding that unlit cigarette between my teeth, not lighting it, just letting it sit there while I talked—putting the thing that could kill me in my mouth but not letting it win.

I showed Hazel the trophies and autographed sneakers in my room, told her which ones were mine from basketball and which were just 'cancer perks'—she looked at them like they meant something, but I had to make it clear: those weren’t real victories.

I sat next to her on the bed after she needed to rest—her breathing was heavy, she joked about fainting—and when I asked if she was okay, she smiled, and for a second it felt like we were just two normal people, not patients.
I told Hazel I’d emailed Van Houten’s assistant and got a real response—her face changed instantly, like she couldn’t believe it was possible.
After reading the letter, I told her to check her inbox—she jumped up so fast, breathless, and I just smiled because for once, I’d done something that truly reached her.
I saw her text saying she couldn't see me anymore, that she was a grenade—like she was trying to push me away to keep me safe.
I told her to stop flirting with me after her serious message—because I couldn't let her see how much it hurt, but I needed her to know I wasn't letting go.
I remember hearing Hazel's voice crack on the phone, that quiet 'kind of' when I asked if she was crying—it hit me right in the chest, and I just knew I had to see that damn swing set for myself.
When she finally said it was about her being a grenade, I didn’t flinch—because I already knew, and I wasn’t going to let her push me away with that logic.

I stood there in my black suit with a cigarette hanging from my lips, watching Hazel step out in that pale blue dress—she took my breath away, and when I told her she looked gorgeous, I meant it more than words could say.

I wore the suit because it felt right—like I was dressing for something real, not just pretending. When Hazel looked at me in that dress, I remember thinking how strange and beautiful it was that we could have this moment, here, like we weren’t carrying so much weight.

We clinked glasses and drank champagne that tasted like something impossible—like stars, the waiter said—and for a second, I wasn’t sure if any of it was real. I just knew I wanted to say thank you, not just for coming, but for being here with me like this.

I remember the weight of her leaning into me, just slightly, as we sat on the bench with my arm around her—us not needing to say anything while the elm seeds floated down and the water shimmered with the city’s lights.

I remember sitting on that bare couch, the room so empty it felt like a stage set, and saying 'thank you' to Van Houten—my voice cracking a little—because I still wanted to believe this pilgrimage meant something, even as he ignored us and sipped his scotch like we were nothing.

I remember the way Van Houten finally looked at me—'Augustus Waters?'—like he’d only just noticed I existed, and how I answered 'It's 11am' instead of asking for the answers I really wanted, because even then, I was trying to hold onto some control in a moment that was already slipping away.
I told her I’d write her a sequel—better than anything that drunk could come up with, full of blood and guts and sacrifice—just to make her stop crying.
I held her close and told her she didn’t spend her Wish on that man—she spent it on us—like that somehow made it okay.
I told her it was above my knee, trying to warn her before things went further, but she just kept kissing me like it didn’t matter at all.
She said she loved me first—really clearly, right there on the bed—and I remember laughing a second before saying it back, still tangled up in her oxygen tube.

I told her about the PET scan, how it lit up like a Christmas tree—my chest, my liver, everywhere—and I tried to hold it together, but I couldn’t. I let myself cry, just for a second, right there on that bench.
After everything fell apart, I asked if it would be ludicrous to kiss her—and she didn’t say a word, just kissed me hard, like we could hold onto each other despite all of it.
I wasn’t there when they told her, but I know the moment it changed for her—when her dad didn’t offer the usual empty comfort, and she let herself really feel it.
I asked Hazel to write my eulogy, and when she said 'It would be an honor,' I felt something crack open—just a little—under all the jokes and the port in my chest.
I told Hazel I was thinking about oblivion, and how I used to believe I’d have some grand story that everyone would remember — and I could see right away that it upset her.
After she called me out, I apologized and pulled her back down, then raised my cup to toast — 'It's a good life, Hazel Grace' — and for a moment, it really felt like enough.
I called Hazel from the gas station in the middle of the night, my voice barely holding together, and asked her to come help me because I didn’t know what else to do.
I pressed my hands to my belly, blood and fluid leaking out, and begged Hazel not to call anyone—just to look, to see it, to witness me like this.
As the ambulance moved, I held Hazel’s hand and whispered, 'Read me something,' because I didn’t want to face the dark alone.
I came home from the hospital, and I could barely make it inside—Hazel was there, helping me, but I couldn’t even stand straight. I didn’t say much, just let her hold me up.
I called Hazel and asked if she had written the eulogy, then told her to meet me at the Literal Heart of Jesus—after I said I loved her, I hung up, not waiting for a reply.
I asked Hazel to speak at my funeral while sitting in the church, and she kissed me like it was the easiest yes in the world.
I smiled when Isaac started reading his eulogy, but I didn’t get to hear all of it—I was already slipping away, eyes closing, holding on to the feeling of Hazel beside me.
I remember the weight of not being there at the end, how my body failed me before I could say everything I needed to say.
I’m in the coffin, wearing the suit from Oranjee. Hazel comes up, breaks down for a second, then composes herself. She whispers, 'It’s ok, you hear me? It’s ok,' and kisses my cheek.

She slips the pack of Camel Lights into the coffin—right between me and the lining—quick, furtive, like it’s our last secret. I can almost taste the unlit cigarette, the thing that killed me, now resting with me like a twisted trophy.
I arranged for Van Houten to come to my funeral, to tell Hazel that life comes from life—even if I couldn’t say it myself.

memories.memory_text: I remember standing there, telling the doctor how she eats so little and never goes out, how she just sits and reads that same book over and over—my voice felt tight, like I was trying to hold something together just by speaking it into place.
I said 'Get in the car' after Hazel mocked the idea of support group again—I could feel my voice cut through the room, firm and final.
I said 'Love you' to Hazel as she got out of the car, and she said it back—her voice soft, like she was tired but trying.
I called out 'Make some friends!' after her as I got back in the car, and she just shook her head—didn't even turn around.
I ran my fingers through Hazel's hair while she lay in bed, struggling to breathe, trying to soothe her as the fluid filled her lungs.
I saw Hazel with a new book, one I hadn’t seen before, and when I asked if it was from him, she joked about herpes like it was nothing—but I could tell she was trying too hard to act casual.
I saw Hazel's phone buzz. She looked excited, then disappointed. I said I was sure he'd call. She said she wasn't worried. I didn't say anything after that.
I saw Hazel actually eating dinner—really eating—and when Michael and I looked at each other, I felt it, that quiet relief. I said it then: I told you Support Group was a good idea.
I heard Hazel shout and I ran into her room, heart pounding, thinking something was wrong with her health—her oxygen, maybe, or she was in pain again.
I had to tell her we couldn't go to Amsterdam—I saw the hope in her eyes and I couldn't give it to her, not because I didn't want to, but because we just don't have the money.
I said no to Hazel’s request about Gus’s gift, even though she pushed back—I could hear the disappointment in her voice, but I had to hold the line.

Hazel turned to me and said, 'So you'll come too,' and suddenly it wasn't just about her anymore—it was about me, about a trip I'd never thought I'd get to take, and I could feel Dr. Maria's eyes on me, waiting.
I rushed into Hazel's room and saw her screaming, shaking, holding her head — I grabbed her right away and waved at Michael to call for help, I couldn't waste a second.
After Michael left to make the call, I stayed holding Hazel, rocking her, telling her it would be okay — that whatever this was, it would end.
I held Hazel close, feeling her breath against me, and told her this was just a thing we could live with—because I needed her to know it wasn’t the end.
I held Hazel's hand and asked her if she was ready, my voice shaking—she nodded, so small in that bed.
I whispered that I wouldn't be a mom anymore—she wasn't supposed to hear, but I think she did.
I tucked Hazel in, pulled the blanket up just under her chin like she liked it, and told her we’d be right outside—close, but not crowding her.

I told Hazel we were going to Amsterdam, even though I wasn’t supposed to say anything until her father got home. The look on her face—like she didn’t even dare hope it was true—made my chest tighten.
She couldn’t get to me fast enough to hug me, so I stepped forward and held her. I could feel her shaking a little, like she was trying not to cry—or maybe like she finally let something go.
I was making breakfast when Hazel came in, already dressed and bursting with excitement—she shouted 'Amsterdam!' and I echoed her, the word feeling like a promise we were finally keeping.
I heard Gus's voice raised inside the house, and without thinking, I put my arm around Hazel and turned her back toward the car—she didn’t need to hear that, whatever it was.
I told Hazel I never made it to the park because I liked watching her sleep—she gave me that look, the one that says I’m not living enough, but I couldn’t leave her alone in this strange room.
I told her about the reservation at Oranjee and saw her hesitate, so I jumped in with 'Let's get you dressed!'—my voice sounded too eager, but I needed her to go, to have this night.

I opened the door and saw Gus standing there in that sharp black suit, cigarette in his mouth, and I remember thinking he looked like he was ready for something real—so I said, 'Looking sharp,' and called Hazel because she needed to know he was here.

I remember staring at the words on Hazel’s shirt—'This is not a pipe'—and thinking it was nonsense, because to me, it clearly was a pipe, until she explained it wasn’t, not really, just a drawing, and I realized she saw the world in a way I couldn’t keep up with anymore.
I stood up and said I’d stretch my legs, knowing they needed time alone—Hazel looked confused, but I had to give them space.

I grabbed Hazel's shoulders when she tried to leave—she wasn't eating, and I couldn't let her go like that, not with how thin she was getting. I just kept saying she had to eat, even as she shouted that she was dying and would leave me behind.
After she yelled it out, I froze—I couldn't believe she'd heard me say I'd be nothing without her. I sat down with her, trembling, tears in my eyes, realizing she'd been carrying that fear all along.

I walked into Hazel's room with Michael at 4 a.m., saw her sitting up in bed with the phone still off the hook, her face already breaking—she already knew. I didn’t say anything, just climbed onto the bed and held her as she fell apart.

memories.memory_text: I sat on the exam table, my legs dangling, repeating 'I'm not depressed' while Mom listed off everything I did wrong and the doctor ignored me, like my words didn't even matter.

I said I wasn't depressed, but the doctor just talked over me, calling it a 'journey' like it was some kind of adventure—Mom and he had already decided for me, and I could tell there was no point fighting it.
I said, 'You can't make me,' even though I knew they would win — it was just another stupid support group they thought would fix me.
Before leaving, I pretended to stab myself in the stomach with an invisible sword — a dumb joke, but it was the only way I could make myself move.
I walked right into him—this impossibly good-looking boy—and all I could manage was a clumsy 'Ooph. Sorry!' before he smiled and said it was okay, but I couldn't even form a real sentence.
For a second, everything just stopped—we were staring at each other and I couldn’t move or speak, like the world had narrowed down to just him watching me with that faint smile.

I locked eyes with that boy—Augustus—and refused to look away, even though his stare made my skin prickle. I won that stupid silent contest without blinking, and for a second, I felt something sharp and real cut through the numbness.

I don’t remember exactly when I raised my hand, but Patrick’s surprise told me it was out of character. The words about oblivion just came out—cold and clear—and for once, I didn’t care if it scared people.

He just looked at me and said, 'Because you're beautiful,' like it was the most natural thing in the world. I froze—I didn’t know what to do with that. No one had ever said it to me before, not like that.

He kept staring, not looking away, like he actually saw me—really saw me—and didn’t flinch. I wanted to look down, to disappear, but part of me wanted to let him keep looking, like maybe I could believe it if he said it long enough.
I remember the needle, the cold table, the pressure in my neck—and then just one sentence, spoken like it was final: Stage IV thyroid cancer.

I remember lying in that hospital bed, gasping like a fish out of water, and knowing I couldn't fight it anymore—Frannie stroking my hair, Dad’s voice cracking as he dialed 911, and then the cold fear that this was it.

I told Augustus I got my GED, and he called me a college girl like it meant something—like I wasn’t just a sick kid skipping school. I remember the way he smiled, and how I shoved his arm, light and easy, like I wasn’t afraid to touch him.
I told him 'An Imperial Affliction' was my favorite book, my voice a little unsteady, like saying it out loud made it too real.
Our hands brushed when he reached for the book, just a second too long, and he teased me about my cold hands—my skin tingled even after he pulled away.

I sat down outside, dialed Gus like we were just going to talk about the book again, and then—this awful sound came through the phone. I didn’t recognize it at first, but it wasn’t him saying he was fine. It was something else. 'What the -- are you ok?' I said, because I didn’t know what else to say.

I saw Isaac upside down in that gaming chair, tears streaming down his face, surrounded by empty cans and trash—he looked so broken, and when he finally spoke about Monica not saying 'always' back, I remember feeling how helpless words can be in moments like that.

When Gus said 'Pain demands to be felt,' I lit up because it was from my favorite book—and then he winked at me, like we were sharing something no one else could touch, a secret world built from words.
I sat up so fast when Augustus started reading that email—my heart pounded like it might break out of my chest. Could it really be from Van Houten? After all this time?
I couldn't breathe—I just kept saying 'keep reading' over and over, hanging on every word. Then I jumped up to check my inbox, desperate to see it for myself.

I typed out that email to Van Houten, my fingers hovering over the keys at first, then finally writing—asking about Anna's mom, the Dutch Tulip Man, Sisyphus—like it mattered, like I deserved an answer.
We kept saying 'ok' on the phone, over and over, neither of us hanging up, and then he said maybe 'ok' could be our 'always'—and I said it again, softly, like it could mean something real.

I saw his name in my inbox and clicked—my heart just stopped when I read 'Should ever you find yourself in Amsterdam, do pay a visit.' I whispered it out loud, like if I said it wrong it might disappear.

I asked Mom if we could go, and she looked at me like she wanted to say yes so badly—but then she said we didn’t have the money. I told her to forget it, but I could see the pain in her face, and it made me feel worse than before.
I told him I used my wish on Disney World and Epcot, and he just threw his hands up like it was the most ridiculous thing ever—he said it was the saddest thing he’d ever heard.
He said he had a crush on me, and I froze—I didn’t know what to do, so I looked away, but I could feel my face burning.

I heard my dad telling Gus how sick I am, how I'll always be sick, and I couldn't let him keep painting me as this fragile thing—not tonight—so I stepped in and asked Gus if he was ready, cutting my dad off mid-sentence.

I remember turning to Mom after Dr. Maria said no, and saying, 'So you'll come too'—just like that, as if it had already been decided, because if she came, they couldn’t use 'what if I get sick' as an excuse anymore.
I asked if I could still go to Amsterdam, and Dr. Simmons just laughed at me—then they all told me I was too sick, like it was that simple.

I read Lidewij’s email and couldn’t believe it—she was still expecting us in Amsterdam. I called for Mom, my voice cracking, needing to know if this was real, if the trip wasn’t actually canceled like I’d assumed.

After Mom finally told me we were really going, I screamed 'I LOVE YOU SO MUCH!!' and barely managed to hobble into her arms. Then, as soon as she left, I grabbed my phone and texted Gus—just that little smiley face—and felt something I hadn’t in a long time: hope.
I stepped out of the bathroom in my pale blue dress, heart pounding, and asked if I was under-dressed—then heard him say I looked gorgeous, and for once, I let myself believe it.
I asked if I could see him, but she said no — that they had to be a family now, and I understood, even though it felt like being shut out when I needed to be close.
I sat in the same chair Gus once sat in while waiting for me — I noticed it right away, how we'd switched places, and I just stayed there, quiet, like holding onto something that mattered.

I stood up, my voice shaking with anger because he kept talking about oblivion and being remembered like none of this—like *us*—was enough. I told him I’d remember him, I’d love him, wasn’t that supposed to matter?
He handed me another Pooh cup and said, 'It's a good life, Hazel Grace,' so softly—I couldn’t stay mad. I clinked my cup to his, and for a moment, I let myself believe it was enough.

I remember the smell hitting me first—vomit and blood—when I opened his car door, and seeing that tube leaking from his belly while he begged me not to call 911, his hands shaking, crying like he was breaking apart, and I just kept thinking, I can't fix this, I can't fix this, so I dialed anyway even though he said he’d never forgive me.

dialogue_exemplars: "And of course, if ever you do decide to write anything else, even if you don't want to publish it, I'd love to read it. Frankly, I'd read your grocery lists. Yours with great admiration, Hazel Grace Lancaster. Age 16."
Lonely, Vaguely Pedophilic Swing Set Seeks Butts of Children.
Augustus Waters was the great star-crossed love of my life. Ours was an epic love story, and I won't be able to get more than a sentence into it without disappearing into a puddle of tears.

I'll spare you the gory details of Patrick's ball cancer. Basically, they found it in his nuts, cut most of it out, he almost died, but he didn't die, and now here he is - divorced, friendless, addicted to video games, exploiting his cancertastic past in the heart of Jesus - "literally" - to show us that one day - if we're lucky - we could be just like him.

I want more numbers than I'm likely to get, and God, I want more numbers for Augustus Waters than he got. But, Gus, my love, I cannot tell you how thankful I am for our little infinity. You gave me a forever within the numbered days,and for that I am eternally
grateful. I love you.

I can't! I can't stay healthy because I'm not healthy, Mom. I am dying. I am going to die and leave you here alone and you won't have me to hover around and you won't be a mother anymore, and I'm sorry, but I can't do anything about it, ok?! Just leave me alone!

You think the only way to live a meaningful life is for everyone to love you, for everyone to remember you. Well guess what, Gus, this is your life. This is all you get. You get me, and your family, and this world. And if that's not enough, well I'm sorry, but it's not nothing. Cause I'll remember you, I'll love you -- You're right -- And I just wish... I just wish you'd be happy with that. You're right. I'm sorry.
Like all real love stories - ours will die with us, as it should. I'd hoped that he'd be eulogizing me, because there's no one I'd rather have...

Dear Mr. Peter Van Houten, my name is Hazel Grace Lancaster. My friend Augustus Waters, who read your book - at my recommendation - just received an email from you at this address. I hope you will not mind that he shared that email with me.
One of the less bull-shitty conventions of the cancer genre is the convention known as the "Last Good Day..."
The problem, of course, is that there's no way of knowing that your last good day is your "Last Good Day." At the time, it's just another decent day.
I didn't believe a word, of course. But that was ok. Funerals, I'd decided, aren't for the dead. They're for the living.

I just wanna say... there will come a time when, you know, all of us are dead. It might be tomorrow. Might be a million years from now but... it's gonna happen. And when it does, enough generations will come and go, there'll be no one left to remember Cleopatra. Or Mozart. Or Muhammad Ali, let alone any of us, right?
Keep `em coming. I can take it. I'm like the Keith Richards of cancer kids.
Oblivion's inevitable. And if that scares you, well, I suggest you ignore it. God knows it's what everyone else does.
